mainTopic: Separating meat and cheese (cleaning the mouth and waiting time), checking one's property, and the rules of washing hands before and after a meal.
overview: The amud opens by explaining what בית שמאי and בית הלל mean by wiping the mouth (מקנח) and rinsing it (מדיח) between meat and cheese. After two explanations are rejected, the גמרא concludes that both sides require both, so there is no real argument. It then examines רבי זירא's rule that wiping is done with bread and adds several limits: wheat, cold, and soft. The final הלכה, though, is that almost any food works for wiping, except flour, dates, and vegetables. Next, רבי יוחנן rules that no waiting is needed after cheese before meat. רב חסדא rules that after meat, cheese is forbidden, and that meat stuck between the teeth still counts as meat. מר עוקבא describes waiting from one meal to the next, and his father's full day. The shared phrase 'vinegar, son of wine' then leads to שמואל's advice to check one's property daily, which the stories of אביי and רב אסי confirm. Finally, the גמרא turns to washing hands at a meal: מים ראשונים are a מצוה and מים אחרונים a חובה. It then covers where the water may land and whether it may be hot or cold, and רבי ינאי begins a limit that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: First suggestion: each side needs only its own method
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that בית שמאי require only wiping, and בית הלל require only rinsing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we say that בית שמאי hold one wipes the mouth and does not need to rinse, and בית הלל hold one rinses and does not need to wipe...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is trying out a first explanation of the argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל. It is setting this up so it can test it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אילימא ('if you say') warns us that this explanation is only a suggestion and will probably be rejected. Here each side holds that its own method is enough and the other method is not needed at all.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If you say', which brings a suggestion that usually gets rejected
Wipes the mouth clean by chewing solid food

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think this is the גמרא's final answer. אילימא always introduces an attempt that the גמרא tests and usually throws out.

phrases.english: If we say that Beit Shammai say:
one wipes and does not need to rinse,
and Beit Hillel say:
one rinses and does not need to wipe.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the explanation of the ברייתא's words מקנח and מדיח.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do מקנח and מדיח mean in the argument?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each side requires only its own method and not the other.

steps.title: Challenge: then רבי זירא would follow בית שמאי
steps.stepSummary: If בית הלל do not require wiping, then רבי זירא's rule about wiping with bread would follow בית שמאי, which is unlikely.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then רבי זירא's statement, 'wiping the mouth is only done with bread', whose opinion does it follow? It would follow בית שמאי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the first suggestion. It uses רבי זירא's rule about wiping to show the suggestion cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא gives a practical rule about how to wipe the mouth. That only makes sense if wiping is part of the הלכה. If only בית שמאי require wiping, רבי זירא would be following בית שמאי against בית הלל. We don't normally rule that way, so the first suggestion falls.

keyTerms.meaning: Wiping out the mouth with food
'Like whom?' — which opinion does this follow?

phrases.english: But that which Rabbi Zeira said:
wiping of the mouth is only with bread,
in accordance with whom? In accordance with Beit Shammai!
phrases.notes: The point is that the הלכה goes like בית הלל, so a practical rule about wiping shouldn't depend on בית שמאי alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the first suggestion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first suggestion, that בית הלל do not require wiping
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי זירא's practical rule about wiping would then follow only בית שמאי, against בית הלל, and that is unlikely.

steps.title: Second suggestion: בית הלל require rinsing too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that בית שמאי require only wiping, while בית הלל require wiping and rinsing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, בית שמאי say one wipes and does not need to rinse, and בית הלל say one must also rinse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new explanation that fixes the problem from רבי זירא, because now everyone agrees wiping is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אף ('also') changes everything. בית הלל now agree that wiping is needed, and they add rinsing on top. So רבי זירא's rule about wiping fits everyone, and the argument is only about whether rinsing is also needed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather', which brings a new explanation after the old one failed

phrases.english: Rather, Beit Shammai say:
one wipes and does not need to rinse,
and Beit Hillel say: one also rinses.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: מְקַנֵּחַ וְלָא בָּעֵי מֵדִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected first suggestion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each side requires only its own method.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sides require wiping; בית הלל add rinsing.

steps.title: Challenge: it would belong on the list in עדיות
steps.stepSummary: If בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict here, this case should have been listed among the 'leniencies of בית שמאי and stringencies of בית הלל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then this is one of the cases where בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict. So it should be taught together with the list of those cases!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second suggestion. It points to a known list of unusual cases that this case would belong to, but it is not on that list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually בית שמאי are the stricter side. There is a special list of the rare cases where בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict. Under the second suggestion, this case would be one of those rare cases. Since it isn't on the list, the second suggestion must be wrong.

keyTerms.term: קוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וְחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל
keyTerms.meaning: The list of rare cases where בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict

phrases.english: then it is one of the leniencies of Beit Shammai
and the stringencies of Beit Hillel,
so let him teach it alongside

phrases.aramaic: קוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וְחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל!
phrases.english: the leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel!
phrases.notes: This is the famous list in מסכת עדיות of the few cases where בית שמאי are the lenient side.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָוֵי לֵיהּ מִקּוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּמֵחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the second suggestion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second suggestion, that בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Such a case belongs on the list of בית שמאי's leniencies in עדיות, but it is missing from that list.

steps.title: Final answer: both require both, and there is no argument
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי mention wiping and בית הלל mention rinsing, but each agrees the other method is also needed. They do not really argue.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, בית שמאי say one wipes, and the same goes for rinsing. בית הלל say one rinses, and the same goes for wiping. Each one mentioned one thing, and they don't disagree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final explanation: both sides require both wiping and rinsing, and they only mentioned different parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: והוא הדין ('and the same is true') means each side agrees to the method it didn't mention. This answers both challenges. Wiping is required by all, so רבי זירא fits. And there is no leniency of בית שמאי, so nothing is missing from the list in עדיות.

keyTerms.meaning: And the same law applies to

keyTerms.term: מָר אָמַר חֲדָא וּמָר אָמַר חֲדָא
keyTerms.meaning: This one said one thing and that one said another

steps.whatToRemember: Final explanation: both בית שמאי and בית הלל require wiping AND rinsing the mouth between meat and cheese. Each one only mentioned one of the two, so there is no real argument.
steps.confusionAlert: Even though the ברייתא is written as 'בית שמאי say... בית הלל say...', which looks like an argument, the גמרא concludes they actually agree.

phrases.english: Rather, Beit Shammai say: one wipes,
and the same is true of rinsing,
and Beit Hillel say: one rinses,
and the same is true of wiping.

phrases.aramaic: מָר אָמַר חֲדָא, וּמָר אָמַר חֲדָא,
phrases.english: One Sage said one thing, and one Sage said another,
and they do not disagree.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: מְקַנֵּחַ, וְהוּא הַדִּין לְמֵדִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the second suggestion and answers both challenges.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: there is no real argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בית שמאי and בית הלל argue about which method is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both require wiping and rinsing; each mentioned only one.

steps.title: Back to רבי זירא's rule: wiping only with bread
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to רבי זירא's statement, which was quoted earlier along the way, to discuss it on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the statement itself: רבי זירא said that wiping the mouth is only done with bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי זירא's rule, which it brought earlier only as part of a challenge. It is setting up a detail about that rule in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גופא tells us we are now studying a statement that was quoted earlier, this time for its own sake. The rule is that wiping the mouth must be done with bread, not with just any food.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': going back to discuss a statement that was quoted earlier

phrases.english: The matter itself: Rabbi Zeira said:
phrases.notes: This is the same statement quoted back in step 2.

phrases.english: wiping of the mouth is only with bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion of a statement quoted in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wiping the mouth must be done with bread.

steps.title: Only wheat bread, not barley bread
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא's rule applies to wheat bread. Barley bread does not work for wiping.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies to wheat bread, but barley bread does not work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רבי זירא's rule: only bread made of wheat counts for wiping the mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: והני מילי ('this applies only') limits the rule we just heard. 'Bread' here means wheat bread. Barley bread is left out and does not work for wiping.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only to

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's rule is that wiping the mouth is done with bread. The גמרא limits it to wheat bread, not barley bread. Step 10 gives the final הלכה, which is broader.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the first of several limits on רבי זירא's rule. The final הלכה in step 10 ends up much broader.

phrases.english: And this applies only to wheat bread,
but with barley bread – no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי בִּדְחִיטֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי זירא's rule from step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only wheat bread works for wiping the mouth; barley bread does not.

steps.title: Wheat bread works only when it is cold
steps.stepSummary: Even wheat bread only works for wiping when it is cold. Warm bread sticks and does not clean.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with wheat bread, we only said it works when the bread is cold. Warm bread sticks to the mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another limit to רבי זירא's rule about wiping the mouth with bread. Wheat bread only works if it is cold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 already ruled out barley bread. Now even wheat bread is narrowed: warm bread is soft and sticky, so it clings instead of cleaning the mouth.

phrases.english: And even with wheat bread, we only said it
with cold bread,
but with warm bread, it sticks.
phrases.notes: Warm bread clings to the roof of the mouth, so it doesn't actually wipe anything clean.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְחִיטֵּי נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further limit after Step 7's wheat-only rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wheat bread wipes only when it is cold, not warm.

steps.title: The bread must also be soft, not hard
steps.stepSummary: Cold wheat bread works only if it is soft. Hard bread does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to soft bread. Hard bread does not work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more limit: the bread must be soft.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the bread has to be wheat and cold. Now it also has to be soft, because hard bread does not clean the mouth well.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two limits. Warm bread is too sticky, and hard bread is too stiff. The bread that works is cold and soft.

phrases.english: And this applies only to soft bread,
but with hard bread, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּרַכִּיכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another condition on top of Step 8
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only soft bread works for wiping. Hard bread does not.

steps.title: Final rule: everything works for wiping except flour, dates, and vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The final הלכה: any food counts for wiping the mouth except flour, dates, and vegetables.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: any food works for wiping, except flour, dates, and vegetables.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical rule about קינוח, wiping the mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After all the bread limits, the הלכה turns out broad: almost any food works for wiping. Only three foods are left out: flour, dates, and vegetables.
steps.whatToRemember: In practice, any food works for wiping the mouth except flour, dates, and vegetables.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical bottom line for cleaning the mouth between meat and dairy.

phrases.english: And the halacha is that with all foods there is wiping,
except for flour, dates, and vegetables.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא בְּכֹל מִילֵּי הָוֵי קִינּוּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion of what works for wiping
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All foods work for קינוח except flour, dates, and vegetables.

steps.title: How long must one wait between meat and cheese?
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי asks רבי יוחנן how long one must wait between eating meat and eating cheese.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי asked רבי יוחנן: how long should a person wait between meat and cheese?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts. רב אסי asks how much time must pass between eating meat and eating cheese.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was cleaning the mouth. Now the question is about waiting time. As it is worded here, the order is meat first and then cheese.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַסִּי מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan:
How long should one wait between meat and cheese?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַסִּי מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: waiting time rather than wiping
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The required waiting time between meat and then cheese.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן answers: no wait at all
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that no waiting time is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: no time at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers that there is no need to wait at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the question was about meat followed by cheese, this answer sounds surprising. The גמרא is about to question it.

phrases.english: He said to him: Not at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: וְלֹא כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 11

steps.title: But רב חסדא says after meat you may not eat cheese
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. רב חסדא rules that after meat one may not eat cheese, though after cheese one may eat meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב חסדא said: if someone ate meat, he may not eat cheese. If he ate cheese, he may eat meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי יוחנן's 'no wait' answer by quoting רב חסדא, who rules the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא draws a line: meat followed by cheese is forbidden, but cheese followed by meat is allowed. So 'no wait at all' after meat seems to clash with an accepted rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (a word that opens a challenge)
But isn't it so that... (brings a contradicting source)

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rav Chisda say:
If he ate meat, he is forbidden to eat cheese,
but if he ate cheese, he is permitted to eat meat!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's answer in Step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that no wait is needed between meat and cheese
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא says that after meat, cheese is forbidden. So saying no wait is needed after meat contradicts him.

steps.title: The question was really about cheese followed by meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רב אסי's question: he asked about cheese and then meat, and for that there is no wait.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he asked: how long should one wait between cheese and meat? He answered: no time at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the problem by flipping the order in רב אסי's question. He was asking about eating meat after cheese.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the question is about cheese first, רבי יוחנן's 'no wait at all' fits exactly with רב חסדא's rule that after cheese you may eat meat. Nothing in רבי יוחנן's answer changes, only how we understand the question.
steps.whatToRemember: After cheese there is no wait before meat. After meat, cheese is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כַּמָּה יִשְׁהֶה בֵּין גְּבִינָה לְבָשָׂר?
phrases.english: Rather, he asked: how long should one wait between cheese and meat?
He said to him: Not at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כַּמָּה יִשְׁהֶה בֵּין גְּבִינָה לְבָשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13 by rereading the question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the question: the order of the foods is reversed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב אסי asked about meat followed by cheese, which would contradict רב חסדא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אסי asked about cheese followed by meat, and for that no wait is needed.

steps.title: Looking at רב חסדא's rule on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now studies רב חסדא's rule by itself: after meat cheese is forbidden, after cheese meat is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the main point. רב חסדא said: if someone ate meat, he may not eat cheese. If he ate cheese, he may eat meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רב חסדא's rule, which was quoted along the way, to discuss it directly. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is quoted again word for word. This time it is the main subject, so the גמרא can ask about its details.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': going back to discuss a statement quoted earlier

phrases.english: Returning to the matter itself, Rav Chisda said:
If he ate meat, he is forbidden to eat cheese,
but if he ate cheese, he is permitted to eat meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up רב חסדא's rule, first quoted in Step 13, to discuss it directly
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After meat, cheese is forbidden. After cheese, meat is permitted.

steps.title: What about meat stuck between the teeth?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יוסף asks רב חסדא whether meat left between the teeth counts as meat for this rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יוסף asked רב חסדא: what is the law about meat that is between the teeth?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יוסף asks רב חסדא about leftover bits of meat stuck in the teeth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether those leftover pieces count as 'meat' under רב חסדא's rule. If they do, cheese would be forbidden while they are still there.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר יוֹסֵף לְרַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yosef said to Rav Chisda:
Meat that is between the teeth, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר יוֹסֵף לְרַב חִסְדָּא: בָּשָׂר שֶׁבֵּין הַשִּׁינַּיִם מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a detail of רב חסדא's rule from Step 15
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether meat stuck between the teeth counts as meat, so that cheese is forbidden.

steps.title: A פסוק shows meat between the teeth is still meat
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers with a פסוק that calls food between the teeth 'meat', so it still counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He read about it the פסוק: 'The meat was still between their teeth.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers by quoting a פסוק that calls the food between the teeth 'meat'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה itself calls what is between the teeth 'meat'. So leftover meat in the teeth still counts as meat, and cheese is not allowed while it is there.

keyTerms.meaning: He read about it (he answered by quoting a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Meat stuck between the teeth still counts as meat for the rule against eating cheese after meat.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the ban on cheese after meat covers leftover meat in the mouth too, not only meat you are eating right now.

phrases.english: He read about it
"The meat was still between their teeth."

steps.triggerLanguage: קָרֵי עֲלֵיהּ הַבָּשָׂר עוֹדֶנּוּ בֵּין שִׁנֵּיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Meat between the teeth is still called meat, so cheese is forbidden while it is there.

steps.title: מר עוקבא compares his waiting time to his father's
steps.stepSummary: מר עוקבא says his father waited a full day after meat before eating cheese, but he himself waits only until the next meal.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר עוקבא said: In this matter I am like vinegar compared to wine when you compare me to my father. My father, if he ate meat at this hour, would not eat cheese until this same hour tomorrow. But I only avoid cheese at the same meal. At a later meal, I do eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: מר עוקבא shares his personal practice for waiting between meat and cheese and compares it to his father's stricter practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the topic of רב חסדא's rule that after meat you may not eat cheese. מר עוקבא gives a measure: his father waited a full 24 hours, while he waits only until the next meal. He calls himself 'vinegar, son of wine' to admit that his practice is less strict than his father's.

keyTerms.meaning: Vinegar, son of wine. A weaker product of something greater. Here it means 'I am less than my father.'
Another meal, meaning a later, separate meal

steps.confusionAlert: מר עוקבא is not saying that his father's practice is the required law. He is describing his father's extra strictness and admitting that his own practice is less strict.
steps.whyThisMatters: This statement is a main source for the custom of waiting from one meal to the next after eating meat before eating dairy.

phrases.english: Mar Ukva said:
I, in this matter,
am vinegar, son of wine, compared to Father,
phrases.notes: He means he is weaker than his father, the way vinegar is a spoiled form of wine.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִילּוּ אַבָּא כִּי הֲוָה אָכֵיל בִּשְׂרָא הָאִידָּנָא,
phrases.english: for Father, when he would eat meat at this hour,
would not eat cheese
until tomorrow at this same hour.
But as for me,
it is only at this meal that I do not eat cheese;
at a different meal, I do eat it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא: אֲנָא, לְהָא מִלְּתָא, חַלָּא בַּר חַמְרָא לְגַבֵּי אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical time measure for רב חסדא's rule that cheese may not follow meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא waits from one meal to the next after meat before eating cheese. His father waited a full day.

steps.title: שמואל compares how often he checks his property to his father
steps.stepSummary: שמואל uses the same 'vinegar, son of wine' expression: his father checked his property twice a day, while he checks it only once.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: In this matter I am like vinegar compared to wine when you compare me to my father. My father would go around and check his property twice a day, but I check it only once a day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second statement that uses the same expression, now about checking one's fields and property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link to the previous step is the shared phrase 'vinegar, son of wine', not the topic of meat and cheese. שמואל admits he is less careful than his father about watching over his property.

keyTerms.meaning: He went around and checked his property and fields

phrases.english: Shmuel said: I, in this matter,
am vinegar, son of wine, compared to Father,
for Father would go around checking his property
twice a day,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנָא לָא סָיַירְנָא אֶלָּא חֲדָא זִימְנָא.
phrases.english: but I check it only once.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֲנָא, לְהָא מִלְּתָא, חַלָּא בַּר חַמְרָא לְגַבֵּי אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same expression as מר עוקבא, but about a different topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל checks his property once a day. His father checked it twice a day.

steps.title: שמואל's teaching that checking property daily pays off
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that שמואל cared about checking his property because he taught that someone who checks it every day will find a coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל follows his own reasoning here. שמואל said: Whoever checks his property every day will find a coin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why שמואל made checking his property a daily habit. It ties this to another teaching of his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לטעמיה' means that שמואל is acting in line with a rule he taught elsewhere. 'Finding a coin' means that checking daily saves you from losses, so it ends up being worth money.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning, meaning consistent with a view he holds elsewhere
A coin of small value, called an אסתירא

phrases.english: Shmuel follows his own reasoning, for Shmuel said:
Whoever checks his property every day
will find a coin.
phrases.notes: He means checking every day saves you from losses, so it is like finding money.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל לְטַעְמֵיהּ, דְּאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind שמואל's daily checking from Step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who checks his property every day will profit and avoid losses.

steps.title: אביי catches his sharecropper carrying wood
steps.stepSummary: While checking his property, אביי meets his sharecropper carrying a load of wood. The sharecropper claims it is going to אביי's house, and אביי tells him that the רבנן's advice already beat him to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי used to check his property every single day. One day he met his sharecropper carrying a bundle of wood. אביי asked him: Where are these going? He answered: To the Master's house. אביי said to him: The רבנן already got here before you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows שמואל's advice working: because אביי checked his fields, he stopped wood from being taken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sharecropper was really taking the wood for himself. When he was caught, he said it was for אביי. אביי's answer means that the רבנן's advice to check your fields every day got there first and stopped the theft.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharecropper, someone who works another person's field for a share of the crops
The רבנן got here before you

phrases.english: Abaye would go around checking his property
each and every day.
One day he met his sharecropper
who was carrying a bundle of wood.
He said to him: Where are these going?
He said to him: To the Master's house.
He said to him: The Sages already got here before you.
phrases.notes: The sharecropper meant to keep the wood. אביי is saying that the רבנן's advice to check daily stopped him in time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי הֲוָה סָיַיר נִכְסֵיהּ כֹּל יוֹמָא וְיוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing that שמואל's teaching from Step 20 is true.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's teaching that checking your property daily saves you from loss
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of אביי catching his sharecropper with the wood

steps.title: רב אסי stops a flood and finds שמואל's coins
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי checked his property daily and wondered where שמואל's promised coins were. Then he found a burst water channel flooding his land, blocked it with his cloak, and called people to seal it. He said he had now found all of שמואל's coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי used to check his property every day. He said: Where are all these coins of מר שמואל? One day he saw a burst water channel flooding his land. He took his cloak, rolled it up, and stuffed it into the hole. He shouted, and people came and sealed it. He said: I have found all of מר שמואל's coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story. רב אסי doubted that checking daily paid off, until one check saved his field from flooding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first רב אסי saw no gain from checking daily. When he caught the flood in time, he understood that one saved disaster is worth all the coins שמואל promised. The story closes this side topic by confirming שמואל's teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: A break or burst, through which water was pouring

steps.whatToRemember: מר עוקבא waited from one meal to the next after meat before eating cheese, while his father waited a full day. Through the shared phrase 'vinegar, son of wine', the גמרא moves to שמואל's advice to check your property every day, and the stories of אביי and רב אסי prove that it pays off.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַסִּי הֲוָה סָיַיר נִכְסֵיהּ כֹּל יוֹמָא,
phrases.english: Rav Asi would check his property every day.
He said: Where are
all these coins of Mar Shmuel?
phrases.notes: He means: I check every day, but I don't see any benefit yet.

phrases.english: One day he saw a water channel
that had burst open onto his land.
He took his cloak, rolled it up,
and placed it inside the opening.
He called out loudly,
people came and sealed it.
He said: I have found
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

phrases.english: all the coins of Mar Shmuel.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַסִּי הֲוָה סָיַיר נִכְסֵיהּ כֹּל יוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story supporting שמואל's teaching, this time from someone who first doubted it.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's teaching that checking your property daily is like finding money
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב אסי catching the flood in time and saving his field

steps.title: First waters are a מצוה, final waters are an obligation
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר אשיין rules that washing before the meal is a מצוה, but washing after the meal is a חובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רב יצחק בר אשיין: washing hands before the meal is a מצוה, and washing hands after the meal is a חובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic about washing hands. It brings a ruling that ranks the washing after the meal as stronger than the washing before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two levels are set up here. A מצוה is a good deed you are supposed to do. A חובה is a firm requirement. Surprisingly, the washing after the meal (מים אחרונים) is placed on the higher level.

keyTerms.meaning: First waters: washing hands before eating bread
Final waters: washing hands after the meal, before ברכת המזון
A good deed you are supposed to do
A firm obligation, stronger than a plain מצוה

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said
Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan said:
The first waters are a מצוה,
phrases.notes: "First waters" means washing your hands before the meal, before you eat bread.

phrases.english: and the final waters are an obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין, אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַשְׁיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the stories about checking one's property to a new topic: washing hands at a meal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מים ראשונים are a מצוה, and מים אחרונים are a חובה.

steps.title: A ברייתא calls both first and final waters an obligation
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that both the first and the final waters are a חובה, which seems to contradict רב יצחק בר אשיין.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this from a ברייתא: the first waters and the final waters are both a חובה, and the middle waters are optional.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling from Step 23 with a ברייתא that calls the first waters a חובה, not just a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יצחק בר אשיין put the first waters on a lower level than the final waters. The ברייתא seems to put them both on the same level, a חובה. That looks like a direct contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: Middle waters: washing hands during the meal, between courses

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
The first waters and the final waters are an obligation,
the middle waters are optional.
phrases.notes: The "middle waters" are a washing done during the meal, between one course and the next.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling from Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יצחק בר אשיין's claim that מים ראשונים are only a מצוה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא uses the word חובה for the first waters too, so they seem to be just as binding as the final waters.

steps.title: Compared to something optional, a מצוה is called an obligation
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא calls the first waters a חובה only because it is comparing them to the optional middle waters.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a מצוה is compared to something optional, the ברייתא calls it a חובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The word חובה in the ברייתא is relative, so there is no real contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is contrasting the first waters with the middle waters, which are fully optional. Next to something optional, a מצוה looks like a requirement, so the ברייתא calls it a חובה. That does not mean the first waters are as strong as the final waters, so רב יצחק בר אשיין's ruling still stands.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the first waters became a full חובה. The ברייתא uses the word only because it is comparing them to the optional middle waters.

phrases.english: A מצוה, when compared to something optional,
he calls it an obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִצְוָה לְגַבֵּי רְשׁוּת חוֹבָה קָרֵי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word: חובה in the ברייתא is a relative term.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא calls the first waters a חובה, the same as the final waters.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first waters are a מצוה. They are called חובה only when compared with the optional middle waters.
steps.whatToRemember: מים ראשונים are a מצוה, and מים אחרונים are a חובה. When the ברייתא calls the first waters a חובה, it only means they are not optional.

steps.title: The full ברייתא: where the water may be poured
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the whole ברייתא. The first waters may be poured into a vessel or onto the ground. For the final waters, the ברייתא comes in two versions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the ברייתא itself: the first and final waters are a חובה, and the middle waters are optional. For the first waters, you may wash with the water falling into a vessel or onto the ground. For the final waters, you may wash only into a vessel. Some say the wording is: for the final waters, you may not wash onto the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back and quotes the full ברייתא from Step 24. The rest of the ברייתא adds a new rule about where the washing water may land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part repeats what we already saw. The new part is about where the water falls: for the first waters it may land anywhere, but the final waters have a restriction. The ברייתא is reported in two versions, "only into a vessel" and "not onto the ground." This sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: "The thing itself": the גמרא goes back to study a source it quoted earlier

phrases.english: The matter itself:
The first waters and the final waters are an obligation,
the middle waters are optional.
For the first waters, one may wash

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בִּכְלִי בֵּין עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע,
phrases.english: either into a vessel or onto the ground,
for the final waters, one may wash only into a vessel,
and some say it this way:
one may not wash onto the ground.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא quoted in Step 24 and quotes it in full.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first waters may be poured into a vessel or onto the ground. The final waters may be poured only into a vessel (or, in the second version, not onto the ground).

steps.title: What is the difference between the two versions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the two versions of the ברייתא lead to any practical difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether "only into a vessel" and "not onto the ground" ever give different rulings. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance, the two versions sound like the same rule. The גמרא wants a real case where following one version would give a different ruling than following the other.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means the two versions of the ברייתא about the final waters.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the two versions quoted at the end of Step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where the two versions of the final-waters rule would rule differently.

steps.title: The difference is wood chips
steps.stepSummary: The two versions differ over pouring the final waters onto wood chips lying on the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: wood chips.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two versions differ when the water is poured onto thin wood chips.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wood chips are not a vessel, but they are also not bare ground. The version that says "only into a vessel" would not allow them. The version that says "not onto the ground" would allow them, since the water does not land on the ground itself.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them

steps.whatToRemember: Final waters: the version "only into a vessel" does not allow wood chips, but the version "not onto the ground" does allow them.

phrases.english: The difference between them is wood chips.
phrases.notes: He means pouring the water onto wood chips lying on the ground. They are not a vessel, but they are not bare ground either.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ קִינְסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The versions differ over wood chips: forbidden by "only into a vessel," allowed by "not onto the ground."

steps.title: Hot or cold water for first and final washing
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: מים ראשונים may be hot or cold, but מים אחרונים must be cold, because hot water softens the hands and does not remove the grime.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the first washing, you may use hot or cold water. For the final washing, you may use only cold water, because hot water softens the hands and does not take off the grime.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the same ברייתא. Now it teaches what temperature of water is allowed for each washing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two washings have different jobs, so they have different rules. The final washing is meant to clean dirt off the hands, and hot water does not do that well because it softens the skin. So only cold water works for מים אחרונים.

keyTerms.meaning: Soften or loosen (the skin of the hands)
Grime, greasy dirt left on the hands from food

steps.whyThisMatters: The reason given (removing grime) shows that מים אחרונים is about cleaning the hands. That is why the water has to be the kind that actually cleans.

phrases.english: For first waters, one may wash
either with hot or with cold water;
for final waters, one washes only with cold water,
because hot water softens the hands
and does not remove the grime.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַיִם רִאשׁוֹנִים נוֹטְלִין בֵּין בְּחַמִּין בֵּין בְּצוֹנֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes quoting the ברייתא whose earlier lines were quoted in step 26 and discussed in steps 27-28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מים ראשונים may be hot or cold. מים אחרונים must be cold, because hot water does not remove the grime.

steps.title: רבי ינאי limits when hot water is allowed for first washing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line about מים ראשונים again, and רב יצחק בר יוסף in the name of רבי ינאי begins to explain that hot water is allowed only in a certain case.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the line 'For first waters, one may wash with hot or cold water': רב יצחק בר יוסף said in the name of רבי ינאי, 'They only taught this where the hand does not...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks one line of the ברייתא to examine more closely. רבי ינאי starts to add a limit to the rule that hot water is fine for מים ראשונים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא seemed to allow any hot water for the first washing. The words לא שנו אלא show that רבי ינאי is narrowing the rule to one kind of case. The details of that case continue right after this section.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of: a formula that limits a rule to a narrower case

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ברייתא. The גמרא repeats the line from step 29 on purpose, so that רבי ינאי can explain and limit it.

phrases.english: "For first waters, one may wash
either with hot or with cold water":

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי:
phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef said in the name of Rabbi Yannai:
They taught this only
in a case where the hand does not...

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first half of the ruling in step 29 and starts to limit it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hot water is allowed for מים ראשונים only in a limited case, which starts with 'where the hand does not...'. The rest of the sentence comes after this section.
